name: quiche
instructions:
A french-leaning quiche, now on ATK's custard ratio (experimentally better than the Julia Child ratio this recipe used before — see notes). Standard 9-inch pie plate format. TWO VARIANTS: A is the mushroom-nutmeg quiche, B is the leek-chorizo quiche.

CUSTARD (ATK RATIO): 5 EGGS to 2 CUPS LIQUID — specifically 1 CUP HEAVY CREAM + 1 CUP WHOLE MILK.

THE CHEESE RULE (BOTH VARIANTS): ALWAYS put the SHREDDED CHEESE ON THE BOTTOM — scattered over the crust before the filling and custard. Soft melting cheeses only: cheddar, monterrey jack, or similar — NOT PARMESAN.

=== VARIANT A — MUSHROOM + NUTMEG ===

- CHEESE BASE: preferably MONTERREY JACK.
- FILLING: sautéed mushrooms (cooked DRY — see moisture note). SKIP THE SPINACH AND THE PARSLEY.
- TOP: freshly grated NUTMEG dusted over before baking (see nutmeg note).

=== VARIANT B — LEEK + CHORIZO ===

- CHEESE BASE: preferably CHEDDAR.
- FILLING: SAUTÉED LEEKS + CHORIZO.
- TOP: NOTHING.

=== PROCEDURE ===

1. Preheat oven to 350°F.
2. Unroll the pie crust and press it into a 9-inch pie plate, crimping the top edges.
3. PREP THE FILLING: variant A — slice and sauté the mushrooms until soft AND until the released liquid has fully evaporated (moisture control is load-bearing — see notes). Variant B — sauté the leeks; cook the chorizo.
4. Whisk together 5 eggs, 1 cup heavy cream, 1 cup whole milk, salt, and pepper.
5. Scatter the shredded cheese over the crust FIRST, then the filling over it.
6. Pour the egg mixture over top.
7. Variant A: dust the top with freshly grated nutmeg. Variant B: nothing on top.
8. BAKE AT 350°F FOR 40 MINUTES. Don't be scared of it puffing — you want it COMPLETELY BAKED.
9. Let cool 5-10 min before slicing and serving.
notes:
=== QUICHE WON — THE FRITTATA IS RETIRED ===

The marcella frittata was retired (September 2026): quiche always comes out better — the crust protects the ends from being burned — for only slightly more effort. The egg-bake slot in the cookbook belongs to this recipe, with italian tortes (Tegliata di Biete) as the future direction for eggs. Leftover eggs, when they happen at all, go to scrambled.

=== THE ATK RATIO — ADOPTED OVER JULIA CHILD'S ===

ATK's quiche ratio: 5 EGGS : 2 CUPS LIQUID, the liquid split as 1 CUP HEAVY CREAM + 1 CUP WHOLE MILK. Experimentally found BETTER than the Julia Child ratio (3 eggs : 1.5 cups) this recipe ran on before.

Ratio history: the original article's 6 eggs : 3/4 cup was way too eggy (baked-omelette-in-a-crust); Julia's 3 : 1.5 corrected it; ATK's 5 : 2 with the cream/milk split is the current standard.

=== CHEESE — ALWAYS ON THE BOTTOM; SOFT MELTERS ONLY, NOT PARMESAN ===

ALWAYS put the shredded cheese on the bottom — over the crust, under the filling and custard. The cheese slot takes soft melting cheeses: CHEDDAR, MONTERREY JACK, or similar soft cheese — NOT PARMESAN (clashing). The variants have preferences: MONTERREY JACK for the mushroom quiche (A), CHEDDAR for the leek-chorizo quiche (B).

=== NUTMEG ON TOP (VARIANT A) — THE 'MAKES IT TASTE MORE EXPENSIVE' MOVE ===

Dust the top with freshly grated nutmeg before baking. This is the single most under-appreciated move in the whole recipe. Nutmeg on cream-based egg dishes is a classical french technique (also see: bechamel, gratin dauphinois) — a background warm-spice depth that ties dairy + egg together and reads distinctly french.

FRESH-GRATED IS BETTER THAN PRE-GROUND: pre-ground nutmeg loses its volatile oils fast and reads flat. A whole nutmeg + microplane sitting in the spice cabinet is a real quality-per-dollar upgrade. If you only have pre-ground, use it, but plan to upgrade eventually.

Don't overdo — a few passes of the microplane across the top is enough. The goal is a background elevator, not a distinctive nutmeg flavor.

Variant B takes NOTHING on top.

=== MOISTURE CONTROL IS LOAD-BEARING (SAME LOGIC AS THE FRITTATA) ===

MUSHROOMS MUST BE COOKED AND DRY BEFORE THEY GO IN: mushrooms release a lot of water when they cook. If you put raw mushrooms into the quiche, the water they release ends up in the custard and the middle stays wet while the edges over-bake. Sauté the mushrooms in a little butter or oil until softened AND until all the released liquid has fully evaporated — then they're safe to add. The leeks in variant B get sautéed first for the same reason. Same rule as tomatoes/zucchini in the marcella frittata.

=== NO GREENS IN THE QUICHE — MAKE THEM A SIDE SALAD INSTEAD ===

Mixed greens and spinach used to live in this recipe (mixed greens primary, spinach secondary). Both removed and moved to clashing — variant A explicitly SKIPS THE SPINACH. In-quiche greens don't do much for the flavor — the cheese + filling + custard base is already the flavor structure, and greens folded into the custard are mostly filler that doesn't contribute much beyond visual color.

BETTER PATH: if you want greens with the quiche, make them a SIDE SALAD instead. A simple dressed side salad (mixed greens or spinach with a light vinaigrette — see dijon-vinaigrette or cream-vinaigrette) alongside the quiche is a natural and classical pairing. The greens do their job better on the plate next to the quiche than folded into it.

=== BAKE IT COMPLETELY — 350°F FOR 40 MINUTES; DON'T FEAR THE PUFF ===

350°F for 40 minutes. DON'T BE SCARED OF IT PUFFING — you want it COMPLETELY BAKED. (This replaces the old just-set-with-a-jiggle guidance that came with the Julia ratio.)

COOL 5-10 MIN BEFORE SLICING: not just for handling. The custard needs the rest period to firm up enough to slice cleanly. Cutting immediately gives you weepy wet slices even from a properly-baked quiche.

=== SIBLING RECIPES ===

- marcella-frittata: the italian egg-and-cheese-and-vegetables sibling. Skillet-to-oven low-heat covered set instead of pastry crust; same moisture-control rules for the vegetables that go in. Read that recipe's failure-mode notes for context on why cooked-and-dried vegetables matter.
- mushroom-leek-galette: french pastry + mushrooms, similar savory-french-pastry family. Different format (rustic folded galette vs pie-plate quiche).
- butter-pie-crust: the from-scratch pie crust recipe if you want to make it yourself rather than buy pre-made.
